output.title: Decreasing Students’ Stress Through Time Management Training

scenes.narration: University students often feel stressed, and this study asks whether a short time management training can reduce that stress and improve control of time.
scenes.layout_description: A student sits surrounded by papers and a clock, with orange arrows pointing toward a calmer path.
scenes.visual_prompt: Minimal hand-drawn university student at a desk with scattered papers, a wall clock, and a small orange arrow leading from clutter to a neat planner, cream background, black ink line art, orange and yellow highlights, lots of white space.

scenes.narration: The authors trained 23 undergraduate students and measured demands, perceived stress, and perceived control of time before training, then 2 and 4 weeks later.
scenes.layout_description: Three simple time points appear beside one student group, linked by a thin line.
scenes.visual_prompt: Three small calendar cards labeled by symbols for before, 2 weeks, and 4 weeks, with a group of students in the center and a single training booklet, minimalist ink drawing with orange highlights.

scenes.narration: They used a non-equivalent dependent variable design: stress and control of time should change, while demands should stay unchanged if training mattered.
scenes.layout_description: Two expected changing scales are shown beside one stable scale.
scenes.visual_prompt: A balance-like sketch with two gauges labeled by icons for stress and control moving in opposite directions, and one third gauge staying still, with orange and yellow accents.

scenes.narration: After training, perceived stress decreased and perceived control of time increased, while demands did not change, suggesting the program may help student well-being.
scenes.layout_description: A before-and-after split picture shows calmer posture on the right.
scenes.visual_prompt: Split scene of a stressed student on the left and a calmer student on the right, with a downward arrow for stress and upward arrow for control, cream background, black ink, orange and yellow accents.

scenes.narration: The paper begins by noting that mental health of university students is an increasing concern, and many students report at least moderate stress.
scenes.layout_description: A campus scene centers on one worried student with a large thought cloud.
scenes.visual_prompt: Simple university campus outline with a worried student holding their head, a cloud of scribbles above, and a small orange exclamation mark, minimalist line art.

scenes.narration: The authors say time-related demands like workload, time pressure, and self-organized learning are serious problems for many students and are linked to higher stress levels.
scenes.layout_description: Three icons for student demands cluster around a clock.
scenes.visual_prompt: A clock surrounded by books, a checklist, and a backpack, with orange circles around the clock hands to suggest pressure, hand-drawn black ink style.

scenes.narration: Because of that, time management interventions are recommended as part of student support, yet the authors say research on their effectiveness is scarce.
scenes.layout_description: A small support sign stands beside a thin stack of papers marked as limited evidence.
scenes.visual_prompt: A student support signpost next to a small stack of papers and a magnifying glass, with one highlighted page, minimalist cream background.

scenes.narration: The study aimed to extend that scarce research and test whether effects would stay stable across two follow-up points after training.
scenes.layout_description: One training session leads to two later check-ins along a timeline.
scenes.visual_prompt: A simple timeline with a training icon at the center and two later circles marked by small calendar symbols, orange line connecting them.

scenes.narration: The training was built around prioritizing, goal setting, strategy development, daily planning, and monitoring, all meant to improve control of time.
scenes.layout_description: Five small action icons orbit a planner notebook.
scenes.visual_prompt: Open planner notebook with five tiny surrounding icons: star, target, stepping stones, calendar, and check mark, drawn in black ink with orange highlights.

scenes.narration: Students first reflected on their activities, then set concrete goals, planned steps, thought about obstacles, and finally monitored task completion each day.
scenes.layout_description: A sequence of four simple sketches shows the training flow from reflection to monitoring.
scenes.visual_prompt: Four-panel strip: thinking student, target goal, staircase plan, and checklist calendar, all minimalist line art with yellow highlights on goals.

scenes.narration: The sample came from a medium-sized German university, with students invited through boards, newsletters, and seminars, and the training lasted 4 h.
scenes.layout_description: A campus invitation scene shows flyers leading to one workshop room.
scenes.visual_prompt: University bulletin board with flyers, a newsletter sheet, and a seminar door opening to a small workshop, cream background, black ink, orange accents.

scenes.narration: Of the 48 students who began, 23 completed all questionnaires for the main analyses, and the average age was 23.30 years.
scenes.layout_description: A funnel narrows from the starting group to the final analysis group.
scenes.visual_prompt: Simple funnel diagram with 48 small student icons entering and 23 leaving at the bottom, with a small age tag beside the final group.

scenes.narration: About half of the final sample were female, and most students reported no or little experience using time management strategies before training.
scenes.layout_description: Two small profile icons and a simple experience ladder appear beside the group.
scenes.visual_prompt: Group of student icons with a half-highlighted female symbol and a small ladder showing experience levels, orange and yellow accents.

scenes.narration: The researchers measured time management behaviour, perceived stress using the tension scale, perceived control of time, and demands as the control variable.
scenes.layout_description: Four labeled cards are arranged around a central clipboard.
scenes.visual_prompt: Clipboard with four surrounding cards, each with a simple icon: planner, tense face, clock with hands, and workload stack, black ink line art with orange highlights.

scenes.narration: Time management behaviour was measured with 18 items, perceived stress with five items, perceived control of time with ten items, and demands with five items.
scenes.layout_description: The item counts are shown as neat handwritten numbers beside each scale icon.
scenes.visual_prompt: Four stacked cards with handwritten item counts, each card paired with a tiny icon, minimalist and clean.

scenes.narration: At time 1, time management behaviour correlated positively with perceived control of time, while perceived control of time correlated negatively with stress and demands.
scenes.layout_description: Three arrows connect the first measurement variables in a simple network.
scenes.visual_prompt: A small network diagram with circles for behavior, control, stress, and demands, using orange arrows for positive and yellow arrows for negative relationships.

scenes.narration: After training, reported use of the taught strategies increased significantly by 4 weeks, and it nearly increased at 2 weeks after training.
scenes.layout_description: A rising line climbs from the first to the third measurement point.
scenes.visual_prompt: A simple upward line graph with three points, the last point circled in orange, and a small notebook icon beside it.

scenes.narration: For the main outcomes, there was a significant overall time effect at 2 weeks, and stress was significantly lower than before training.
scenes.layout_description: The stress line drops from the first to second point beside a small statistic symbol.
scenes.visual_prompt: Two-panel mini chart showing a downward stress arrow and a small table-like marker for overall time effect, with orange emphasis on the drop.

scenes.narration: Perceived control of time showed only a tendency at 2 weeks, but by 4 weeks it had increased significantly compared with the pretest.
scenes.layout_description: A delayed upward arrow appears after an initial faint rise.
scenes.visual_prompt: A timeline with a faint upward curve at 2 weeks and a bold upward curve at 4 weeks, highlighted in orange and yellow.

scenes.narration: At 4 weeks, the overall time effect remained significant, and both perceived stress and perceived control of time changed in the expected directions.
scenes.layout_description: Two arrows move away from a central pretraining point.
scenes.visual_prompt: A central starting point splitting into one downward arrow labeled by a tense face and one upward arrow labeled by a clock, minimalist ink art.

scenes.narration: Students with no or little prior experience seemed to profit more from training than those with moderate or some experience, especially for perceived stress.
scenes.layout_description: Two small student groups are shown with different sized arrows of change.
scenes.visual_prompt: Side-by-side groups of students, one with a larger orange arrow and one with a smaller arrow, showing stronger change for the less experienced group.

scenes.narration: The control variable, demands, did not change significantly at either follow-up, which supports the authors' interpretation that training mattered.
scenes.layout_description: A stable gauge remains flat across all three time points.
scenes.visual_prompt: A flat line gauge labeled with workload icons staying level across three points, with only a small orange circle around it.

scenes.narration: In discussion, the authors argue that prioritizing, goal setting, daily planning, and monitoring may have given students more orientation and control.
scenes.layout_description: A student follows a clear path through several small planning markers.
scenes.visual_prompt: A student walking along stepping stones marked with a target, calendar, and checklist, with orange arrows showing direction.

scenes.narration: They also note that the training was short, only 4 h, yet it still had a positive impact in this mixed student sample.
scenes.layout_description: A small workshop clock sits beside a group of different students.
scenes.visual_prompt: Workshop room with a small clock labeled 4 h and diverse student figures around a planner, minimalist black ink with orange accents.

scenes.narration: The authors treat this as a preliminary study because the sample was small and many students dropped out before the second measurement.
scenes.layout_description: A shrinking group of student icons moves toward later time points.
scenes.visual_prompt: A row of student icons gradually thinning across a timeline, with a small warning mark near the later point.

scenes.narration: They suggest future studies should use larger samples, compare time management training with other stress interventions, and test whether effects last longer.
scenes.layout_description: Three future research paths branch from one central question mark.
scenes.visual_prompt: A branching path diagram from a question mark to three icons: bigger group, two different intervention boxes, and a longer timeline, orange highlights.

scenes.narration: Overall, the paper concludes that time management training may help undergraduate students reduce stress and increase perceived control of time, though more evidence is needed.
scenes.layout_description: The final slide shows a calm student beside a simple takeaway statement.
scenes.visual_prompt: A calm student holding a planner with a small upward clock and downward stress arrow, clean minimalist composition, cream background, black ink, orange and yellow highlights.
